nameStory: The Amur maple gets its name from the Amur River valley in the Russian Far East, where this small tree naturally grows wild. This region along the border of Russia and China is where European botanists first discovered and catalogued this distinctive maple species in the 1800s.
description: Amur maple is a small, compact deciduous tree that rarely grows taller than 20 feet, making it perfect for residential landscapes and city streets. Unlike the towering sugar maples we're used to seeing, this Asian native has a shrub-like appearance with multiple trunks and a rounded crown. Its leaves are smaller than most maples, and it puts on a spectacular fall color show with brilliant reds and oranges that can rival any native New England tree.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small three-lobed leaves, much smaller than other maples at only 2-4 inches long. The center lobe is distinctly longer and more pointed than the side lobes, giving leaves an almost trident-like shape. Feel the leaves - they're thinner and more delicate than sugar maple leaves.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays small and compact, rarely exceeding 20 feet tall with a rounded, often multi-stemmed form. Branches grow in an upright, vase-like pattern that's much more contained than spreading native maples.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, fragrant yellowish-white flowers appear in upright clusters in late spring after leaves emerge. The sweet scent is noticeable when you get close to blooming branches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces typical maple 'helicopter' seeds (samaras) but they're smaller than native species and often bright red or pink when young, making them quite showy in late summer.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young that develops shallow furrows with age. The bark feels smoother and stays lighter colored than most mature native maples.

habitat: In New England, Amur maple is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings - residential yards, parks, and along city streets where it was planted as an ornamental tree. It tolerates urban conditions well and thrives in a variety of soil types. Occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found naturalized along forest edges or in disturbed areas near developed land.

seasonality.spring: Small, fragrant yellowish-white flower clusters appear in May after the leaves have emerged, unlike some maples that bloom before leafing out. New leaves unfold with a slight reddish tinge.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with distinctive small three-lobed leaves. The colorful red or pink young seed clusters are often the most noticeable feature during late summer.
seasonality.fall: Puts on one of the most reliable and brilliant fall color displays of any maple, turning intense shades of orange, red, and sometimes yellow. Fall color often appears earlier than native maples.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the compact, upright growth form and smooth gray bark. Small buds and fine branching pattern help distinguish it from larger native maples.

funFact: Despite being from Asia, Amur maple is actually more cold-hardy than many of our native New England maples and can survive temperatures down to -40°F, making it tougher than the sugar maples that define our region's fall foliage!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young red maples, but Amur maple's leaves are consistently much smaller and the tree stays compact rather than growing tall. Memory trick: 'Amur stays small and neat, red maple grows tall to beat the heat.'
contextualKnowledge: Though non-native, Amur maple is not considered invasive in New England like its cousin Norway maple. It was widely planted as a street tree because it tolerates urban pollution and stays small enough not to interfere with power lines.
compareHints: Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe. While red maple can also have three-lobed leaves, they're much larger and more variable in shape, plus red maple grows into a large canopy tree rather than staying compact and shrub-like.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
